messages.subject: simulating multi-state jolly-seber data
parts: I'm struggling to figure out how to stitch together a data simulation for  a multi-state (Chap.9 BPA) and Jolly-Seber (Chap.10 BPA). Specifically, how to deal with individuals entering into the data simulation. Can all individuals enter at time= 0 (i.e. creating a dummy first encounter period, like in the analysis step), and then let the entry probability sort out when each individual is first encountered, or should I try to specify the time of first encounter for individuals as is given in the examples of Jolly-Seber models?

messages.subject: Re: simulating multi-state jolly-seber data
parts:
Hi Tim,


I believe Dan works around the not yet entered state in his simulation code. He releases a certain number of individuals per year as a function of entry probability (b) and a multinomial distribution


# this line

releases <- rmultinom(1, N, b)


They can then enter as 1s (alive and breeding), and survive, breed, skip breeding, and die following entry using a simplified (3x3) state-transition matrix rather than a 4x4. If you aren't interested in secondary detection occasions or breeding probabilities then a lot of that code can be removed. If you want to include the whole matrix then just follow Table 2 in Dan's manuscript.


Dan is a super helpful guy, might be easiest to contact him!

messages.author: 40e173783f466ae0
messages.subject: Re: simulating multi-state jolly-seber data
parts:
I'm curious if there are examples of a MSJS where individuals can enter the population in more than 1 state?  In my case, I'm working with goose banding data where individuals can be captured as HY or AHY. I thought I had it figured, but it seems not. I'm starting to re-think my entire approach to the simulation & model. If anyone has suggestions I'd be grateful.

I started simulating separate populations of HY and AHY individuals, with their own separate vectors of entry probabilities (but an un-entered HY can only enter as a HY; it can't 'age' and enter as an AHY). But this is causing some problems:

  1. It's not clear how to simulate a population that's growing/ declining. Should HY individuals be the only ones with entry probabilities, after t=1, so all the individuals that are only encountered as AHY have actually been in the population, just not observed?
  2. How to set the initial states at t=1. Some simulated HY individuals are encountered as HY, others not until AHY. Should the initial state be based off of what gets observed, all fixed to the un-entered HY state, something else?
  3. The 'augmented' population. Should there be a separate # of augmented individuals for the HY & AHY state, or just 1? This has implications for setting that initial state at t=1.
I recognize that choices at one level here will dictate what happens at others (like if un-entered individuals can age without entering). 

I'm open to any ideas anyone might have and I'd be happy to share my code thus far off-message board.

Thanks in advance for any suggestions.

messages.author: f7b0e875c85b25ba
messages.subject: Re: simulating multi-state jolly-seber data
parts:
Have you thought about approaching this as almost a temporary emigration model, but in reverse order? So basically, HY could recruit directly into the observable population as you would expect in a normal JS model and then age into AHY. Or, HYs could recruit into this unobservable, languishing state, and from that state recruit into the observable population as AHY, or in theory languish forever without ever fully recruiting. In a nutshell, the temporary emigration parameter is place between being born and fully recruited, and would represent the probability that an individual that, although alive, was not available to recruit into the population. . I haven't fully vetted this idea yet, but I think if you had secondary detection information, the model is fully identifiable. If you don't, the HY detection probs will be confounded with the temporary non-recruited parameter. If are you interested in exploring this approach, I can send you a rough work up. This is one of those situations that setting up the initial latent state is easy enough in the land of simulations, but I can imagine will be a real headache when applied to real data.

The data simulation and model structure would look something like this:


where f is the entry probability, beta is the temporary pre-recruitment parameter, and phi j and a are the hy and ahy survivals. And the states represent: 1) Entry into superpopulation; 2) Pre-recruitment; 3) Observable as HY; 4) Observable as AHY; and 5) dead

This approach, if it works, would resolve points 2 and 3, as all individuals would be allowed to start as off spring, but enter at different points in their life into the correct age class.

In terms of point 1, it's a little tricky to simulate a population that is growing or shrinking at the rate you want it to when you aren't explicitly modeling temporal variation in N, but my suggestion would be pick a vital rate (phi or recruitment) and model that temporally as a trend, and see if it gets you close.

e.g., 
n.occs <- 9
mu.rec <- 0.1
g.prime <- rep(NA, times = n.occs -1)
for (i in 1:(n.occs-1)){
  g.prime[i] <- rnorm(1, mu.rec + 0.02 * i, 0.05)
}
fec <- g.prime/sum(g.prime)



Hope this is somewhat helpful!

-Dan
